title: Mary prays (CCC 2617–2619)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus prays: a whole night before choosing the Twelve, thanks before the miracle, not my will but thine. Your line was he prayed first.

Two scenes, close together in Luke's Gospel. In the first, a woman in Nazareth hears an angel's message that will rearrange her whole life, and she answers in one sentence. In the second, she has walked into the hill country to see her cousin Elizabeth, and when Elizabeth greets her, she doesn't answer in one sentence. She sings. A short yes, and then a long song.
screen: `NAZARETH: ONE SENTENCE.` → `THE HILL COUNTRY: A SONG.` → `A SHORT YES, A LONG SONG.`

segments.voice: You've met both scenes before; today the Catechism reads them as prayer. The angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son. She asks how. He answers. And she says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, that be it done is one word: fiat. The Catechism says simply: this is Christian prayer, to be wholly God's, because he is wholly ours. It isn't a request. It's an offering. She doesn't know what comes next, and she says yes anyway. Then the second prayer. Elizabeth calls her blessed, and Mary answers: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin it begins Magnificat, and that's the song's name. The Catechism calls it the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church. It sings that God has scattered the proud, put down the mighty, lifted up the lowly, and filled the hungry with good things. Praise, in Mary's mouth, is not polite. It's a song about the world turned right side up. One more moment: at a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Mary tells Jesus, then tells the servants, "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." The Catechism sees her there asking on behalf of others, and pointing them toward her Son. First yes, then praise, and all along, pointing past herself.
screen: `BE IT DONE TO ME: FIAT.` · `WHOLLY GOD'S.` · `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.`

segments.voice: First the yes: bring to mind one thing you've been resisting, something you can't control, and without solving it, try letting it be; if you pray, borrow Mary's words, be it done to me according to thy word. Then the praise: name, slowly, a few good things that are real today. If you don't pray, let yes and gladness simply sit side by side.
Mary prays. Her fiat at the Annunciation, be it done to me, and her Magnificat at the Visitation, my soul doth magnify the Lord: in Catholic teaching, yes to God, then praise. Today's word.
Your line: yes, then praise. Her yes came before she knew what came next. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics say Mary's fiat in the Angelus, where be it done unto me according to thy word is one of its lines, and the Magnificat is sung or said at Vespers, the evening prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.

chat.says: What makes Mary's prayer different from just asking God for things?
options: Her first prayer is an offering, not a request: be it done to me. Then she praises, in the Magnificat.
Her prayers are only requests for others, like at Cana; she never praises God for herself.
Her prayer was mostly silent; the Gospels record no words of hers spoken to God at all.
chat.meaning: The Catechism calls Mary's fiat Christian prayer: to be wholly God's. Her Magnificat is praise, the song of the Mother of God and of the Church.

Magnificat.meaning: Mary's song of praise, named for its first Latin word

notes: CCC 2617–2619 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). Check: the fiat as Christian prayer in its purest form, 'to be wholly his, because he is wholly ours' (2617); Cana (2618); the Magnificat as the song of the Mother of God and of the Church (2619).
Fiat and Magnificat are Vulgate words ('fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum', 'Magnificat anima mea Dominum'); confirm.
howItsDone: the Magnificat at Vespers is standard in the Liturgy of the Hours; confirm 'every evening' phrasing.
Douay-Rheims Luke 1:38, 1:46–47, John 2:5: confirm exact wording.
Editor: 'Christian prayer in its purest form' (not CCC 2617's wording) replaced with 'this is Christian prayer'; unsourced 'young' cut.

Editor (second pass): trapdoor no longer calls fiat the opening word of Luke 1:38 (the Vulgate answer opens 'Ecce ancilla Domini'; fiat comes mid-sentence); howItsDone's 'every evening' claim softened.

Audit (1132–1141 pass): howItsDone said Catholics pray Mary's words 'in the rosary'; the Hail Mary is Gabriel's and Elizabeth's words to Mary, not hers, so the rosary claim is cut and the Angelus (which does contain 'be it done unto me according to thy word') kept. Luke 1:38, 1:46–47, John 2:5 (Douay-Rheims) and CCC 2617–2619 checked and found accurate.
